<reason>Both sides argued competently, but CON built the more technically incisive case. PRO's opening and closing offered a clean moral throughline (workers already bear the risk; a floor closes an externalized subsidy) and PRO neutralized the "surveillance fortress" charge with a plausible 1099/payroll-tax analogy. However, CON identified a genuine, persistent design tension—PRO's mechanism must be fast enough to help a worker injured days after crossing a threshold, yet light enough to avoid the cross-platform aggregation apparatus PRO itself calls unnecessary—and PRO's answers ("a public administrator," "trailing lookback," "days not tax seasons") never fully closed that gap. CON also sharpened its rationing argument into a "probabilistic hedging" mechanism in Rebuttal 2 that survived PRO's own pressure question about visibility, and PRO's closing rebuttal to that point was assertive rather than analytically engaged. Additionally, PRO's statutory-disclaimer answer to the classification-law risk was contested by CON in Rebuttal 1 but never revisited by PRO afterward, leaving that route live for CON. CON's opening was clipped for length, which is a real execution cost, but the core critiques (gaming, moat, classification) were already stated before the cut, limiting the damage. On balance, CON's rebuttals more precisely targeted PRO's mechanism and left fewer of PRO's counters fully answered than vice versa.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 point that PRO's "remit and aggregate later" fix contradicts the need for real-time coverage for a worker "hurt Thursday" was the most decisive exchange; PRO's later fixes (public administrator, trailing lookback) never fully escaped that tension, and CON's Rebuttal 2 refinement (platforms hedge on aggregate uncertainty even without real-time visibility) closed the loop CON had opened.</best_rebuttal>
